definition: The populace is the ordinary people of a place — the general mass of its residents, as opposed to its elite.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word populace. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know populace should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When grain ran short, the emperor worried less about the senate than about the populace of the capital.
A crowd is a much smaller and briefer thing than a populace — it lasts an afternoon and fills one square, while a populace takes in everyone who lives in the place, gathered or not.
Humanity goes further than a populace: a populace stops at the borders of one city, valley, or nation, while humanity counts every person alive everywhere.

The public is people in their role as audience or customers — you address the public, poll the public, serve the public. The populace is people as the mass of a place's residents: you count it, feed it, govern it.
The citizenry is a place's people seen as holders of civic rights — voters and jurors. The populace is broader and plainer: everyone who lives there, voter or not.

The populace is the broad mass of ordinary people in a place, seen from above and counted in thousands: everyone outside the privileged few.
Rulers, planners, and pamphleteers speak of the populace when they mean the general run of residents rather than any particular person.
neutral / civic — the census and history-book word
Populace names the governed many, and writers reach for it when the view is from above — proclamations, censuses, sieges.
Two neighbors to keep straight: populous is an adjective meaning full of people (a populous city), and a populist is a politician who claims to champion the populace.
The people, the crowded, and the champion — three different words.

In 1854, the harbor city of Veynes hired a young engineer to modernize its waterworks.
The council imagined new fountains for the promenade, where its own villas stood.
The engineer began instead with a count.
Ledger by ledger, she tallied the populace of the city: dockworkers, seamstresses, lodgers, children — every resident, whether or not their names appeared on any voting roll.
Nine in ten residents drew water from four failing wells, while the promenade already enjoyed three fountains.
